scenes.label: Anchor · the lead
scenes.title: A mission changed by ice
scenes.headline: ENDURANCE SPECIAL REPORT
points: The obstacle: a ship trapped in ice
scenes.credit: Sources: Shackleton, South (1919); Royal Museums Greenwich chronology
narration: This is Expedition News Network, with a classroom report looking back at the Endurance expedition.
In 1914, Ernest Shackleton set out to cross Antarctica, but ice trapped his ship before that crossing could begin.
As the ice damaged Endurance, the goal changed from exploring a continent to bringing people home.

scenes.label: Reporter · evidence and conclusion
scenes.title: A route toward help
scenes.headline: CHANGING CONDITIONS. CHANGING PLANS.
scenes.credit: Route schematic, not to scale · based on South, chapters VIII–IX
narration: Shackleton's later account, South, describes supplies being prepared to move before the ship was abandoned.
The party eventually reached Elephant Island, and six men sailed the James Caird toward South Georgia to seek help.
All twenty-eight members of the Endurance party survived, although the wider expedition's separate Ross Sea party suffered losses.
The original crossing was not completed, but preparation and cooperation helped make rescue possible.

items.title: Endurance: from crossing a continent to bringing people home

scenes.label: Anchor · opening
scenes.title: When the mission changed
scenes.headline: ENDURANCE SPECIAL REPORT · 1914–1916
scenes.credit: A present-day classroom report looking back at historical evidence
narration: Welcome to Expedition News Network. Today we are looking back at the Endurance expedition, from 1914 to 1916.
Our question is: how did a plan to cross Antarctica become a mission to bring people home?
Two ideas help explain the story: changing conditions required new plans, and people with different skills had to work together.
First, our research desk explains the original goal.

scenes.label: Research reporter · the changing goal
scenes.title: The ice changed the plan
scenes.headline: THE PLANNED CROSSING DID NOT BEGIN
points: New priority · Keep the party safe
scenes.credit: Royal Museums Greenwich chronology; Scott Polar Research Institute
narration: Shackleton planned to cross Antarctica. Endurance carried his party toward the Weddell Sea, but the ship became trapped in pack ice.
Pack ice is floating sea ice crowded together. The ship drifted with it instead of following the planned route.
When pressure damaged the ship in 1915, the party had to leave it.
That connects a condition to a decision: the damaged ship could no longer provide a safe base for the original mission.

scenes.label: Research reporter · a primary source
scenes.title: Prepared to move
scenes.headline: READ THE WORDS. EXPLAIN THE EVIDENCE.
points: Stores, dogs, sledges, and equipment were ready to be moved from the ship at a moment’s notice.
scenes.credit: Ernest Shackleton, South (1919), chapter IV · October 25, 1915 entry
narration: Here is a short quotation from Shackleton's book South: Stores, dogs, sledges, and equipment were ready to be moved from the ship at a moment's notice.
This detail supports the idea that the group prepared for a change before it happened.
However, this is the leader's account, written after the journey. It helps explain his preparations, but does not tell us what every person thought.

scenes.label: Field reporter · a route toward help
scenes.title: A route toward help
scenes.headline: FROM THE ICE TO ELEPHANT ISLAND
scenes.credit: Classroom schematic · not to scale · South, chapters VIII–IX
narration: Now look at the route diagram. It begins at the Weddell Sea ice camp, then moves to Elephant Island, then to South Georgia.
In April 1916, the party reached Elephant Island in three small boats.
Six men then took the James Caird toward South Georgia to seek help for those who remained.
The arrows show the order of destinations. They are not exact sailing tracks or a measure of distance.

scenes.label: Field reporter · people and purpose
scenes.title: Different skills. A shared purpose.
scenes.headline: PREPARATION CONNECTED PEOPLE’S WORK
scenes.credit: Shackleton, South, chapter IX · The Boat Journey
narration: The James Caird needed preparation. Carpenter Harry McNish worked on the boat, supplies had to fit into limited space, and Frank Worsley's navigation helped guide the crew.
These were different jobs connected to the same purpose: reaching help.
Preparation could reduce some risks, but it could not make the voyage certain to succeed.
This is why our report explains people's work as well as naming the places they reached.

scenes.label: Research reporter · checking our sources
scenes.title: What can each source tell us?
scenes.headline: A STRONG REPORT CHECKS MORE THAN ONE SOURCE
scenes.credit: South; Royal Museums Greenwich chronology and Frank Hurley photo catalog
narration: We compared Shackleton's memoir with a museum chronology to check the order of events.
A Frank Hurley photograph, cataloged by Royal Museums Greenwich, is another kind of evidence about the ship and ice.
A photograph records a visible moment. It cannot prove every cause or tell us what someone felt.
Our newsroom background is an illustration, so we do not use it as historical evidence.

scenes.label: Anchor · conclusion
scenes.title: The crossing failed. The party survived.
scenes.headline: TWO IDEAS EXPLAIN THE STORY
points: Connect people’s skills to a shared goal
scenes.credit: Scope: the 28-person Endurance party · the separate Ross Sea party suffered losses
narration: The remaining Endurance party was rescued from Elephant Island in August 1916. All twenty-eight members of that party survived.
The wider expedition also included a separate Ross Sea party, which suffered losses, so we must be precise about whom we mean.
The planned crossing was not completed. The rescue was a different achievement.
Our evidence shows how changing plans and working together shaped the outcome. Thank you for watching Expedition News Network.
